The veriT format, initially presented in 2010, has undergone continuous development thanks to the effort of numerous researchers and developers. A team from multiple institutions has contributed to its expansion and improvement, focusing on key aspects such as side conditions, if-then-else structures, array operations, and optimization techniques. The format's design has also been refined to enhance its compatibility with existing SMT solvers. This work details the most recent additions to array handling, including extended operations, incorrect function handling, and an overall format optimization. These features were implemented to facilitate the integration of new logic components and to assist in the debugging process.

A pressing concern in large-scale distributed machine learning is balancing efficiency with security. Recent techniques like Knowledge Distillation focus on improving efficiency through knowledge compression, while federated learning ensures data privacy. This research proposes a novel algorithm called FedBuff, which combines Knowledge Distillation and Federated Learning to achieve the best of both worlds. FedBuff enables data efficiency by having the client's full model learn from the server's parameter reductions, while secure training ensures that the server can operate without a significant performance loss. What sets our approach apart is its scalability, as it allows the training set to grow without requiring additional memory, making it possible for a server to accommodate thousands of models without increasing memory usage. In contrast to current knowledge distillation methods, FedBuff provides a clear path for continuous learning while maintaining security. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in multiple machine learning tasks.

This study explores using transfer learning to enhance speech recognition through automatic differentiation and stochastic gradient descent. A distinctive aspect involves pre-training a speaker and language model on transcribed speech from the target language without a known reference, before fine-tuning the model with supervised data. The study also investigates language transfer effects and examines how effective transfer learning performs across languages with varying degrees of similarity. Results from experiments on artificial and real-world languages show that transfer learning benefits speech recognition even when there's no direct relationship between source and target languages, although source languages that are more similar yield greater gains. Further analysis using attention mechanisms reveals that transfer learning attention often focuses on a limited number of source language features.

Underwater environments present significant challenges for robots navigating them, largely due to communication limitations that hinder efficient information sharing between robots. This work introduces a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning framework called SPGP-SARSA, which combines sparse coding for compact policy representation and GPR for precise value estimation, respectively, reducing the inter-robot communication requirement to just occasional value updates. SPGP-SARSA achieves greater efficiency by leveraging sparse coding to rapidly process large state spaces, and further improves time efficiency through a new sampling technique. Evaluations conducted both through simulations and with a physical robot demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in enhancing policy execution speed and accurately handling complex state spaces, while also showing substantial time efficiency gains compared to conventional methods.

The approach to solving a broad class of relativistic stellar models in the context of general relativity is demonstrated. These models, consisting of two fluid components with interrelated pressures and a combined four-force, can be solved upon reducing to a single-fluid model. As a result, we show that solutions for the single-fluid case, such as those by Bardeen, Zheleznov, and Guinter, can be extended to establish corresponding two-fluid solutions.

Although NLP tasks typically involve a substantial amount of labeled data, such tasks sometimes only have a small subset of annotations, particularly in the domain of semantic correction. To address this limitation, we developed a general method for adapting pre-trained multi-task models that has been demonstrated across various domains. Our approach involves fine-tuning the model on the target task using an extended dataset, which includes the available corrected samples, incorrectly labeled data from related tasks, and artificially corrected incorrect sentences. When applied to a semitic language, we found significant improvements over traditional multi-task transfer learning methods. Furthermore, our research indicates that utilizing incorrectly labeled data can actually enhance transfer learning performance. Additionally, the proposed GEC adaptation method can be used without modification for languages with different writing systems.

We introduce two novel approaches to dividing a cake among multiple individuals using the deterministic Round-Robin method. By utilizing a cut-and-choose strategy as the base instead of simple cuts, our algorithm secures an improved fairness standard known as Max-Min Fairness. Our solution features the round-rrobin determination phase with an increased round count, providing an allocation fairness guaranteed within a factor of 2/k of the optimal solution. Furthermore, our algorithm necessitates minimal input regarding individual preferences, specifically the valuation function for any subset of participants, making it applicable in scenarios with limited preknowledge.

Our study of UGC 8839, a low-surface brightness galaxy, utilized the Subaru/MOIRAS HII region survey in the Na I D lines to map its gas distribution and kinematics. We discovered that the galaxy's HII region population is concentrated within a 10-kiloparsect radius, similar to other galaxies. Based on HII location, mass, and kinematic analysis, we found that the galaxy's disk extends over 30 kiloparsects, with bulge or bar features absent. The galaxy exhibits outer disk rotation curves and significant rotation off-set, with gas within 10 kiloparsects showing the same kinematic properties. We estimated the galaxy's total gravity potential and dark matter content, as well as its stellar to gas mass ratio of 0.43. The survey also revealed extensive gas streams in the outer disk, with associated star formation in some areas, but little to no SFG in other regions. Our findings highlighted the importance of local surface density in driving star formation, with a high gas fraction in the outer disk, as evidenced by a low f1D value of 1.35.

Using state-to-state mapping, lattice QCD simulations explored the impact of quark mass changes on pion properties in relation to lattice data. By parameterizing RECOCO functions, researchers were able to create a tool to predict lattice QCD results for various observables across different quark mass conditions. The mapper demonstrated a precise fit to the data with minimal error and revealed that lattice QCD results for pion mass, decay constant, and other metrics are interconnected. Notably, varying the input pion mass leads to proportional changes in other lattice QCD metrics with a fixed ratio, providing a useful framework for interpolating and extrapolating data.

The recent discovery of extreme variability in the accretion rates of two classical T Tauri stars, DO Peg and V1057 Cyg, poses significant challenges to current theoretical understanding.  The extreme variability observed in these stars, particularly in the short time scales of months, contrasts with accretion models that struggle to explain such behavior.  In addition, mass accumulation models predicting extreme behavior in later stages of disk evolution also fall short, as both DO Peg and V1057 Cyg are in the early stages of disk evolution.  The source of a possible power law distribution of accretion variability in smaller time scales and its connection to disk variability in longer time scales remains unclear.  Furthermore, the possible role of magnetic funnels in causing accretion variability requires more research. The SIT framework for offline multi-agent learning aims to enable adaptation to new environments and novel partner behavior while maintaining effective collaboration with existing agents. To achieve this, it creates shared individual trajectories that combine the rewards from all agents, causing each agent to behave as if they are the only one in play, yet are guided by the collective goal. Building on existing techniques, the method employs two neural networks to transform experiences from various agents into unified experiences that capture the best and worst aspects of the current policy. This allows each agent to learn from the more successful and less successful behavior within the suite. Testing shows that in comparison to traditional methods, IT outperforms them significantly in terms of the final performance achieved and shows a strong capacity to adapt to new scenarios and transfer knowledge to new environments.

This study presents multiple variations of a convolutional neural network (CNN) based image registration method, utilizing a single network to determine the transformation that aligns two images. We explore two types of spatial transformations, namely rigid transformations characterized by rotation and translation, and affine transformations, which additionally include scaling and shearing. To evaluate our proposed methods, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation using two publicly available datasets, one synthesized and one real-world, containing eye fundus images exhibiting deformation and misalignment. Furthermore, we incorporate gradient-based optimization refines the CNN-generated solutions. When compared to traditional intensity-based methods, our approach yields notably better results, particularly in cases of complex deformation patterns.

Quantum mechanics' counterintuitive nature is illustrated by nonlocal effects, which defy the expectation that a single particle's behavior should depend only on its local properties. This notion is clarified by expressing single-particle entanglement in second quantization, which reveals that the "entangling" aspect results from comparing different spatial modes, not truly nonlocal phenomena. Conversely, this model can give rise to steering, a genuinely nonpassive effect. To demonstrate this, experiments using photons in different spatial modes can be conducted, where single-particle entanglement and steering effects are examined through detection patterns generated by an intense laser in various arrangements, including those with mirror symmetry, where steering effects are anticipated. These predictions may facilitate experiments capable of observing and characterizing single-particle entanglement and steering in practice.

The integration of Blockchain technology into IoT Vehicles (IoVs) systems presents a promising avenue for enhancing both data security and privacy preservation. IoVs networks are increasingly reliant on cloud services for managing and processing the vast amounts of traffic data captured by onboard cameras and sensors, with blockchain serving as a trustworthy middleware for secure authentication and access control. This article offers a comprehensive overview of blockchain architectures designed for IoVs applications, detailing their operational mechanisms, before exploring both the benefits and limitations associated with these solutions, before looking ahead to potential future enhancements.

This paper introduces a novel pilot efficiency enhancement technique for user equipment feedback in future wireless networks, specifically for a base station serving multiple users in a multiuser MIMO system. Traditional feedback methods, such as pilot clustering, involve significant pilot overhead as they require extensive signal processing and transmission. In an effort to overcome this limitation, we propose a pilot-efficient closed-loop system for a base station that employs an open feedback mechanism, resulting in reduced pilot efficiency costs. In this mechanism, user equipment reports signal quality to the base station, enabling it to select the best signal quality, rather than the base station instructing user equipment to choose the best signal quality, as in traditional methods. In both signal quality estimation via covariance matrix inversion and precoder selection via Lloyd's clustering, our proposed method proves to be more effective than existing techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate in simulation studies that our proposed pilot encoding scheme leads to notable gains in sum rate, while in a typical scenario, it results in an 85% reduction in pilot overhead.

We present an analytical explanation for the surface current robustness observed in the bulk-surface model of the Cramer-Shanks curve, specifically at the interface between the topologically distinct bosonic and fermionic bulk phases. A detailed calculation of these surface currents is also provided. Our current analysis has implications for existing surface current measurements in the BCS boundary layer of surface superconductivity. Furthermore, our calculations yield precise expressions for surface currents in the Moore-Read fermionic bulk phase and the $\nu=5/2$ interferometer, facilitating their direct experimental verification.

In the case of Brans-Dicke theory, we examine the behavior of photons in a spacetime that includes a scalar component, particularly in relation to rotations of compact objects like neutron stars or black holes. For these rotating objects, certain regions of allowed angular velocities exist, and we find that in some of these regions, photons can reach the end of their trajectory with non-zero energy, while in others, they lose all their energy and get trapped near the object. If these regions are distinct, it implies that Brans-Dicke theory could be detected through comparative analyses of pulsar observations, and if they overlap, the same goal can be achieved. Endings to these regions, however, are marked by singularities that resemble those found in general relativity, and we also investigate the angular velocities in rotating solutions of Brans-Dicke theory that allow for these allowed regions to exist.

We investigated the characteristics of a specific category of gravitational waves generated by collapsing Population III binary remnant black holes in the early universe. Using a universal model for the mass distribution of Population III single stars, we calculated the merger rate density of this category of binary black hole events at different cosmic time periods, specifically from 1 to 8 gigayears after the Big Bang. When paired with the Hubble parameter and the cosmic expansion of the universe, we determined the merger rate of these events in the observable universe, peaking at redshifts of 2.1 with a rate of 0.24 per year per cubic gigaparsec. This category of events in the local universe has a rate of $10^{-3}$ per year per cubic gigaparsec, providing theoretical basis for detection by next-generation gravitational wave observatories and for the events that may have contributed to the supermassive binary in the center of the Milky Way.

Simulating open-ended conversational texts requires a systematic approach to generate texts within a consistent context, much like text-based games. To accelerate this simulation process, we present TextWorldExpress, a significant improvement over the initial TextWorld environment through several key enhancements. By introducing a simulated agent with an accelerated thought process and a ninefold increase in throughput, we successfully submitted a top-ranking entry in the AgentThink 2022 Text Game Championship using TextWorldExpress, securing first place with high distinction.

FDHT-LSTM is an innovative hardware efficiency model that combines lifted matrix factorization of the Finite Difference method with a compact Hamiltonian dynamics neural network hardware design. This architecture aims to significantly improve the performance of traditional tensor-decomposed, model-oriented hardware for finite difference methods, which typically involves heavy data movement and high memory access patterns. FDHT-LSTM achieves this by using a finite difference operator factorization method to minimize data precision requirements and constructing a specialized hardware that keeps intermediate values in high-speed registers, thus avoiding memory access. This architecture is particularly effective for high-dimensional problems with time-step sizes greater than 1. The FDHT-LSTM was developed in PyTorch and evaluated on various high-dimensional options with the results showing a substantial increase in efficiency compared to traditional methods, with a up to 40 times greater speed and energy effectiveness for a typical time-step. The FDHT-LSTM was also compared to other platforms and demonstrates the value of combining software and hardware optimizations for complex dynamical systems models.

In $(1,d-1)$-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, self-binding energy is self-defined to explore the WDGC, a concept that reduces to the conventional WGC in Minkowski space. To achieve a formulation that remains valid regardless of the $\Lambda$ value, we propose a generalized charge-to-boundary charge ratio. Calculated explicitly for various theories and particle types, ratios are derived and may have broader implications. Notably, these results suggest that the WDGC could potentially influence the parameter space allowed by general relativity.

Let $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ be a Noetherian local ring of positive characteristic and let $R^\circ$ denote its integral domain. If the first local cohomology module $H^{d-1}(\mathfrak{m}, R)$ contains a non-trivial submodule consisting of elements annihilated by some power of $\mathfrak{m}$, then $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ is not F-rational. Conversely, if $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ is not F-rational, then the localization of $R$ at some prime ideal not equal to $\mathfrak{m}$ will have a similar property. We establish these two distinct results, and demonstrate their relevance in determining when certain rings are F-rational.

This paper delves into the effects of a binary all-or-none order execution in DGP2 redispatch markets as the costs of green energy generation rise. As nuclear energy gives way to cheaper renewable sources, flexible redispatch is required to balance the grid, and our analysis reveals an counterintuitive finding that this flexibility results in a less efficient outcome. To examine the impact of an AN order system, a combined mathematical and simulation-based analysis is performed, which is compared to our initial hypothesis of improved solution space exploration. Furthermore, a simulation of the German electricity market is conducted, uncovering that AN order features lead to higher prices and a redistribution of redispatch costs.

Given an algebraically closed field $K$ with a transcendence degree of $\text{r}$ over its constant field, we examine the absolute Galois group of $K$, denoted as $\Gal( \overline{K} / K^{ \text{ab} })$, in relation to its relation to polynomial equations in multiple variables and their connection to Diophantine problems. In particular, for r = 1, we establish that rerecognition of Galois groups is not feasible and propose that an infinite number of primes cannot R-recognize any finite group, which may have implications for the R-recognizability results by Poonen and Rubinstein (1996) and Suter (2007). Furthermore, we demonstrate that R-recognizability in r = 2 and beyond is closely related to the Polynomal analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture (1966). Ultimately, under the assumption that the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture (1974) holds for specific elliptic curves, we show that the R-recognizability of any finite group is attainable in a specific extension of a polynomial field, denoted as $K(x)$.

Recent observations from the Stratospheric, Thermospheric, and Thermospheric Imaging Spectrograph (ISS) instrument on the Saturnian satellite Titan have revealed peculiar patterns in Saturn's north polar stratosphere.  These observations are in stark contrast to what was previously known about the south pole and instead resemble the distorted vortex patterns observed on Earth.  Initially expected to be dipolar like the south pole, the vortex patterns eventually became tripoidal before collapsing in February 2018.  Notably, high altitude features present in the visible spectrum were absent in infrared observations.  By comparing infrared and visible spectrum images, high latitude heat releases corresponding to these features were identified.  These observations provide strong evidence for quadratic wind dependence in atmospheric heating and imply strong westerly winds at the north pole, in contrast to the predominantly easterly winds observed at the south pole for over three decades.  A simple atmospheric circulation model supports this interpretation and predicts the eventual equatorward shift of the heat release pattern similar to what was observed at the south pole.  This study also provides an explanation for the unusual heat release pattern present in the north polar stratosphere, in contrast to what was previously observed at the south pole, in addition to predicting the eventual eastward movement of the heat release pattern.

We have modified Haraux's recent result on the blow-up of $L^1$-norm of solutions to the semi-linear Schrödinger equation in a bounded domain, where the nonlinearity is of a power type. Due to the inability to use concentration-compactness principles or spherical means methods near the focus time, we employed a local variant of the Morrell-Stoeger estimate to establish the blow-up of the $L^1$-norm under specific conditions. These conditions involve the geometry of the domain, the growth rate of nonlinearity, and the disposal of initial energy. By leveraging the Local Stoeger estimate and the Local Harbrecht-Haraux result, under similar conditions, we obtained the lower bound of the blow-up rate of the $L^p$-norm for any $p\geq1$.

Commutative algebra typically concentrates on characteristic-one or characteristic-specific properties, yet ignoring characteristic-zero yields no significant benefits, as it specifically falls between these characteristics. This approach justifies studying algebraic geometry in characteristic-zero specifically and makes the implementation easier for automated systems.

We have extended the established relationship between double vector bundles and symmetric double vector bundles to a more generalized scenario, involving a symplectic double vector bundle and its corresponding n-fold symmetric vector bundle in the same higher dimension.

In this work, we establish a connection between the natural measures known as Kirillov's measure and the geometric measures on specific Lie algebra structures called $B$-orbits within the dual of a cobracket space, provided the associated Lie group has a specific property known as unimodular. Unimodularity allows for the direct comparison of these two types of measures and enables a demonstration that the geometric measures are directly related to the regular representation of the associated group, which in this case is known as the Heisenberg group. As a consequence of this finding, we obtain a proof that the representation is weakly mixing, regardless of whether it is defined over the rational or real numbers, in comparison to previously known results that only held for the real-numbered version of this Lie algebra.

An efficient phase-retrieval method for experimental data has been developed, leveraging a comparison between the energy-scattered-out-of-an-integer-x-ray-band's tail and the remaining energy-scattered-into-zero, which aligns with diagonal elements of a two-dimensional system's Hamiltonian. The algorithm's superiority in speed and stability over conventional approaches is evident, particularly when dealing with noisy data, allowing for the precise reconstruction of energy-scattered-time-correlation-functions and ultimately enabling the study of liquids' intermediate-density dynamics through x-ray scattering experiments.

This research develops a method to simulate complex patterns of fractures in porous materials, where some areas are completely impermeable and other fractures have varying permeabilities. A key component of our model is the integration of the Dirac-$\delta$ function in a porous media flow blockage model, which is then replaced with an exponential $\eta$-function to represent the varied permeabilities of fractures. The resulting system of equations consists of non-linear partial differential equations coupled with discrete Darcy's law, and we use an iterative finite element method to find approximate solutions. A robust preconditioned iterative solver is employed to efficiently handle the large systems of equations, with spatial discretization achieved through linear finite elements in two dimensions.

A decision-making process is closely tied to hypothesis selection, which is crucial for action selection. Traditional methods often rely on hand-crafted performance metrics to evaluate hypotheses and enable decision-making. However, this approach can be inflexible and prone to human bias. To overcome these limitations, this work introduces a novel framework that utilizes utility functions based on neural networks, seamlessly integrating them into an end-to-end learning process. This design enables the model to choose from multiple hypotheses and learn the corresponding decision-making process in a joint training setting. Furthermore, the proposed method's design permits easy incorporation of human knowledge into utility functions, which can guide hypothesis selection and enhance model performance. This feature is showcased in several mock task scenarios, including gesture recognition and sign language parsing, demonstrating improved performance over baseline methods and highlighting the framework's versatility and ease of use.

Effective natural language understanding relies on identifying semantic relationships between text elements, including predicting functional discourse markers and intrinsic relations between words, phrases, or sentences. To advance these areas, we have created discsense, a vast dataset containing over 1 million rows of discourses consisting of four-sentence four-pair structures with associated discourse relations and pairwise coherence scores. To fill a notable gap in current research, our dataset provides an essential resource for developing and evaluating models for predicting discourse markers, relations, and coherence. We further propose a unified framework that facilitates the joint learning of discourses and coherence, which we have assessed using our dataset. Our findings showcase the effectiveness of our approach, indicating that our discourses and coherence labels provide valuable guidance for machine learning tasks, while also revealing key insights into the complexity of the coherence phenomenon.

In non-Euclidean geometry, geodesics represent the paths between points in space, and their behavior is influenced by the geometric properties of objective functions in factorized settings. This research demonstrates that under certain strong geometric conditions, known as restricted strong convexity and smoothness, objectives in factorized models exhibit well-behaved geodesic properties, ensuring they remain on a specific manifold. This approach is applied to various matrix decomposition methods, including low-rank matrix factorization and non-negative matrix factorization. Furthermore, it finds that under pecking order constraints used in algorithms such as SVD, NMF, and non-negative eigen decomposition, objectives display restricted strong geometric properties. These findings offer fresh insights and may provide new convergence guarantees for both Riemannian optimization methods and gradient updates in matrix optimization problems.

A strong edge-coloring of a graph with the maximum degree \((G, \delta)\) requires a coloring of its edges in a way that any three distinct vertices are connected to edges of different colors in a triangular formation. In 1990, Faudree and Gy\`{a}rfas proposed a conjecture for bipartite graphs, suggesting that the strong edge-coloring number of bipartite graphs with maximum degree 3 is 7. This paper provides a counterexample to this conjecture, presenting a specific infinite family of bipartite graphs with degree 3 that have strong edge-coloring numbers greater than 7. Notably, the first such graph identified in this research appears at the 19th order, which is obtained by modifying the Pr\'{o}ss-Regal graph of order 18.

This study applies co-evolutionary genetic algorithms to a simple coordination game, allowing agents to both learn strategies and adapt assessment methods automatically. Multiple runs of the algorithm exhibit consistent behavior cycles characterized by equilibrium states and distance phases lasting tens of generations. A notable finding emerges from the results, revealing that the expected distance from Nash Equilibrium is smaller in scenarios where agents interact with the most successful population rather than at random, which aligns with analogous human learning experiments. A simple model is created to predict the fundamental dynamics observed across the algorithm's results.

Consider a weighted oriented graph, denoted as $\mathcal{O}^{w}(G)$, which is derived from a weighted graph $G$ by directing its edges in a specific way. In this paper, the authors investigate the conditions under which the ordinary and symbolic powers of the associated edge ideal, $I(\mathcal{O}^{w}(G))^{(r)}$ for $r \geq 1$, are equivalent. They establish sufficient criteria to ensure that for a monomial ideal in a polynomial ring in three variables, the symbolic and ordinary powers are identical. Additionally, they prove the convergence of the sequence of symbolic powers. Furthermore, they examine a specific class of weighted oriented path graphs, $\mathcal{P}^w_n$, and demonstrate the equality $I(\mathcal{P}^w_n)^{(r)}=I(\mathcal{P}^w_n)^{r}$ holds, resulting in symbolic and ordinary powers being identical for any power.

Silent data corruptions, a pervasive and insidious issue in software systems, pose significant problems for developing reliable artificial intelligence. Neural networks are particularly susceptible to this problem due to their sensitivity to even minor alterations in input data, regardless of their significance. Differential uniformity testing is an effective technique for detecting silent data corruptions by identifying cases where changes in input do not produce any changes in output. Our research introduces novel non-uniform range restriction methods that enhance the effectiveness of silent data corruption detection beyond current techniques. By automatically detecting silent data corruptions across nearly 4000 models and integrating automated and manual analysis, our results provide valuable insights into the urgency of addressing silent data corruptions in machine learning. Our methods also demonstrate higher detection rates than existing automation tools and manual testing, with an F-score of 0.429 compared to an score of 0.09 achieved by existing techniques. Our findings reveal that existing techniques frequently fail to detect silent data corruptions in popular computer vision models, particularly when changes occur in specific color channels of input images.

The challenge of tagging names in languages with limited resources is a problem that many researchers are working to solve. To make progress, we proposed an innovative solution called Multilingual Dynamic Attention Network (MDAN). This framework starts by using a multilingual word2vec to represent names and text, then employs attention mechanisms to focus on the most relevant parts of a language's name. MDAN goes further by dynamically adjusting how names in different languages are related to each other, all while considering the specific characteristics of each language. Evaluations on six languages showed significant improvements over current methods, with MDAN boosting performance by 2.3 names per 100 on average, and even greater gains in languages with very little data.

This research examines the behavior of particle ratios including $K^{\pm}/K^{0}_s$, $p/\pi$, and $p/B$ across various experiments involving proton-proton collisions at the Tevatron and Large Hadron Collider, as well as proton-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus collisions, with focus on transverse momentum and system size. The study finds that when the transverse momentum of particles becomes significant relative to the dimensionless parameter $\beta_T$, the ratios of certain particles such as kaons to pions and baryons remain constant in both small and large system collisions. A fit to the data yields the value of this parameter at the 5th percentile as 0.8 GeV/c, with corresponding values for the transition from small to large systems in both hadron and quark-gluon plasma scenarios. The findings also reveal that the relationship between the production of particles begins to change when the total system size becomes comparable to the hadron radius, with implications for understanding the strong interaction force that governs the behavior of particles in these collisions.

The impact of a city's infrastructure layout on the spread of riots has been explored in this research. By integrating the basics of network theory with the spread of phenomena models, we developed the 'City Riots Model' to investigate how removing key infrastructure can influence the dynamics of riots. Using the Boston riots as a case study, we demonstrated how our model can capture and predict the spread of unrest in a specific city layout, and found that the impact of infrastructure removal varies significantly depending on the location of the removed elements.

This research introduces a braced extended regular expression brachr, incorporating Brzozowski's operator from 1964 along with the star operator and containment-checking functionality. We demonstrate a symbolic approach to assessing regular expression containment issues by applying Brzozowski's operator, which involves computing the derivative set of a given expression. This method is based on previous work by Jaffar and Malik from 1991, as well as Schapire's algorithm in 1977. Moreover, we modify the approach by discarding duplicate derivatives and instead use simplified forms, which can significantly improve the efficiency of the algorithm in practice.

Despite the existence of potent VIO algorithms, numerous deep learning-based models, which utilize neural networks, do not explicitly employ features from vibration measurements and angular rates, key outputs of complementary VIO models, traditionally referred to as Kalman filters. Such conventional models have consistently delivered dependable and efficient results in various rigorous, real-world applications. In contrast to these models, deep learning-based approaches stand to gain an advantage if they were to leverage training data comprising rates, along with either image or textural discrepancies. In this study, a combined end-to-end learning framework is developed that cooperates with the existing traditional models and utilizes end-to-end learning techniques to integrate multi-modal data, specifically vibrations and rate measurements. Experimental findings across various rigorous scenarios, both simulated and real-world, have confirmed that such a framework, trained on rathe data, delivers precise and robust estimates with significant improvements in both accumulated positional and angular errors, whereas the conventional models alone do not demonstrate gain from the exclusion of rate and vibration features during the training phase.

We present the higher-order Weyl semimetals in three-dimensional space with both charge exchange and bond exchange distortions applied to a pyramidal lattice model, exhibiting diverse topological features. By distorting the "Weyl-Weyl" anomaly, we discover widespread topological behaviors categorized as deep topological phases and a topological bond spiral. Applying a nonlinear transformation to the pyramidal lattice yields the linear three-dimensional system with Weyl-Hamiltonian representations, revealing diverse higher-order topological phenomena from the Weyl semimetals. This, in turn shows that three-dimensional topological systems can exist in a topological bond spiral state, a "square-root" topological configuration. This study thus provides an integrated framework for understanding different topological disorders.

This research focuses on solving data completion problems in image processing, particularly when large missing sectors are involved. We aim to construct a method that accounts for geometric shape and provides precise solution estimates. Our approach involves selecting an appropriate type of edge finite elements, modified to handle missing data regions. Tests using real images with significant missing data demonstrate that our chosen element type yields superior results compared to other choices, producing results with better geometric accuracy and higher pointwise precision.

Influencing importance is a innovative method designed to rate the influence of each instructor as well as the neuron in order to form a compact and knowledgeable unit. Results from several rounds of testing on diverse tasks confirm the effectiveness of knowing several things at once, particularly in difficult classification tasks.

Quantum quenches in many-body systems lead to inevitable irreversible heating, resulting in the absence of return to the initial state after a finite time. Our research proposes a novel approach that employs an effective temperature to assess the amount of irreversible heat produced, finding a direct proportionality between the growth of irreversible entropy and the temperature coefficient in the Bose-Hubbard model. This relationship holds true even as the system transitions from integrable to non-integrable and eventually into a thermal phase. Our findings may have broad implications for experiments conducted with cold atoms.

We present an alternative perspective on time dynamics beyond standard non-unitary approaches, typically requiring specialized setups. Instead, our approach involves simply treating the initial joint state of the system and its environment as a pure state, then applying time-twirling transformations. As a result, we observe emergent non-unitary dynamics in the system alone. Surprisingly, our approach naturally leads to plausible predictions for non-unitary dynamics in the system, including instances where quantum interference plays a crucial role. Furthermore, our framework enables an alternative derivation of fundamental results such as the Jammer-Mahler non-unitarity theorem and the time-nonlocality of non-unitary dynamics. Additionallly, our approach can be applied in scenarios involving weak measurements, yielding the notion of time-nonlocal distinguishability. Our findings also reveal that non-unitary dynamics become more nonlocal when the initial entanglement between the system and environment is higher. Ultimately, our alternative framework necessitates plausible assumptions and provides a clear path for experimental verification involving the careful preparation of the system-environment joint state, weak measurement of the non-unitarily evolved system, and subsequent tomographic analysis.

This research proof establishes that for any sequence of numbers within the interval (0,1), denoted as τ = (τ_j), a smooth function f can be found within the set of polynomials with degree at most k in n variables that accurately maps the vertices of a specific simple geometric shape, the simplex Δ_n, to the given nodes within the unit cube Q_n. Furthermore, these vectors can be chosen in such a way that they maintain a non-degenerate property, ensuring the simplef f(Δ_n) preserves its original topological characteristics. This result holds true provided the number of nodes in the unit cube satisfies the condition 2^n ≥ 2^n. In addition, these findings have further implications for finite difference methods used for numerical partial differential equations.

Silicon samples with etched surfaces were produced using a chemical etching technique applied to various types of highly doped silicon substrates.  In order to preserve the original carrier concentration, etched samples were then covered with a buffer oxide layer before being fully etched.  In comparing the results, the carrier concentration of the fully etched samples was found to be higher than that of the buffer oxide etched samples, which in turn had a carrier concentration similar to that of the original bulk material.  The increased carrier concentration of the fully etched samples is believed to be caused by the introduction of interstitial silicon during the final etching step.

Interior-exterior cycling within planetary systems is a critical concept, yet its influence on the atmosphere's prolonged evolution is difficult to predict. To address this challenge, we formed a coupled model that integrates a weather process model with a two-dimensional planetary interior-exterior cycling framework. Utilizing this combined model, we examined the interaction between the planet's atmosphere and its ice sheets by investigating its behavior in the short and long term. Through high-resolution simulations, we demonstrated the capacity of the model to accurately simulate the atmospheric components and establish the expected relationships in the short term. In the long term, we found that the planet's interior-exterior cycling could either stabilize a highly volatile atmosphere or give it new energy sources for prolonged development.

In multivariate point process modeling, particularly for point clouds with multiple dimensions, nonlinear models like the Hawkes process are utilized. This model incorporates self and mutual excitation or, alternatively, self and mutual inhibition phenomena. A novel parameter estimation method based on the nonlinear Hawkes process is developed, considering potential process non-renewal due to inhibition. The estimated parameters can capture complex interactions, even after accounting for observed data. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through theoretical examples and simulations. Furthermore, a combination of the Hawkes process and variational autoencoders is proposed for point process classification, achieving successful results in both simulated and real-world application scenarios.

A new concept for a polarizing device suitable for high-power lasers is proposed, termed a plasma waveplate. Its implementation would be feasible using a plasma channel with a thickness that depends to the first order on the square of the wavelength, divided by the product of plasma electron density and magnetic field strength, resulting in a minimal required plasma waveplate thickness of approximately 1 millimeter for a 100 Tera-Gauss magnetic field and a plasma electron density of 10$^{18}$ cm$^{-3}$. Beneficial applications of plasma waveplates may include precise control of laser polarization in the study of non-linear Compton scattering in strong magnetic fields and enhanced generation of circular polarization in plasma channels leading to more uniform acquisition of radiation-electron beam inverse Compton scattering data.

The T2HM model from the two-Higgs doublet version of the Standard Model can explain the tiny electric dipole moment observed in tau leptons, which lies within measured limits. To achieve this, new sources of complex phase in the Higgs sector are introduced, and if their impact is small, they may leave distinct patterns in the expected Higgs boson decay outcomes and the behavior of tau electric dipole moment. Even so, these effects could also manifest in weak interaction currents, producing both scalar and pseudoscalar contributions. As a result, predictions are made for several processes, and calculations are performed for the tau electric dipole moment, tau anomalous magnetic moment, and the ratio of the pseudoscalar to the scalar component in tau decays. Formulas are also derived for the radiative process $\tau^-\to e^-\gamma$ as well as the rare decay $\tau^-\to \mu^-\gamma$.

This paper investigates the error correction capabilities of rank metric codes, focusing on a comparison between the traditional rank metric and its soft variant, particularly in relation to code rates. Through information theoretic bounds and numerical data analysis, distinct similarities and differences in the behavior of these code types at rates both below and above 1/2 are revealed. Notably, both metrics exhibit comparable error correction capabilities at rates below 1/2, whereas the traditional rank metric shows reduced robustness at rates above 1/2 when compared to its soft counterpart.

We investigate the operator product expansion (OPE) blocks of conserved current fields along geodesics within the context of holographic duality in CFT$_2$. Our analysis calculates these blocks within AdS$_2$ using AdS$_3$ geodesic operator frameworks, revealing distinct admissible representations for these blocks in AdS$_2$ compared to Fields of spinless and massive geodesic blocks (which allow only representations parameterized by outer radii). Ultimately, our work demonstrates that current OPE blocks contain a mixture of AdS$_2$ geodesic operator phases that fail to satisfy boundary conditions at the AdS$_2$ horizon, thereby precluding their expression as single geodesic AdS$_2$ operators. Instead, our findings indicate that an AdS$_2$ geodesic operator system must include an additional absorption coefficient, unlike the AdS$_3$ case. Furthermore, our work explores the relationship between these results and the spin of the involved fields.

In 1991, Gelfand and MacPherson established a profound connection between the combinatorial complex of separated partitions and the Gelfand-MacPherson combinatorial differential manifold known as theelm complex. We discover this complex contains a substructure equivalent to the Gelfand-MacPherson combinatorial differential manifold, now called the prouncelm complex. Furthermore, utilizing the fact that theelm complex has a trivial homology property, we conclude the prouncelm complex also exhibits trivial homology, providing a novel approach to proving its null-homologiality.

Earlier SN~II-LS observations had also suggested high Ni~II emission, but these cases were rare and often contested. To determine the precise location of each mirror in a lobster-eye system, we analyzed the azimuthal rotation of cross-shaped images created by X-ray point sources reflected off the micro mirrors. An X-ray telescope called "Lobster-eye" generated these images using a holographic mirror array. By observing the relationship between the source's and the cross-image's rotation angles, we were able to extract positional information from the angular difference. The results demonstrated that this method could determine the absolute position of individual mirrors with an angular precision of 0.5 degrees. Due to this technique's simplicity and high accuracy, it can effectively support maintenance and facilitate functional assessments of lobster-eye telescopes in the future.

Utilizing methodological approaches from our prior work on equations that are fully nonlinear and of a second order, this paper applies a level set formulation to transform the original equation into a boundary value problem with a nonlinear optimal stopping condition, subsequently resolving the resulting problem to derive the desired results.

We have conducted an $\Omega=0.3$ cold dark matter simulation in the context of general relativity, initially using a model with a negligible $\Lambda$-term and a pressureless matter model. We have determined the halo mass distribution as opposed to a density-only approach. The results have been compared to the standard $\Omega=0.3$ halo mass distribution and found the density-only model to predict the halo mass distribution accurately, whereas an $\sim 10%$ discrepancy was observed when initially using a model that incorporates scalar perturbation. We have further investigated the effect of a $\Lambda$-term and general relativistic corrections on the halo mass distribution, initially using a model with a density-only approach, and found their influence to be of a similar magnitude.

The newly developed two-time scale method for analyzing rotating stars with variable densities allows for the investigation of property assignments in a fluid. Unlike conventional methods where properties are expressed as functions of spatial coordinates, this method assigns properties to individual fluid elements, facilitating the analysis of rotating stars with variable densities. As a result, the approach yields analytical expressions for the properties of fluid elements, including mass, angular momentum, and other characteristics. Additionally, the method was applied to the detailed study of a rapidly rotating star, incorporating self-gravity and mass loss, demonstrating its utility in analyzing complex scenarios where fluid elements lose their identity due to magnetic fields or other mechanisms, requiring specifications of properties based on mass, angular momentum, and other parameters.

Acquiring extensive, accurately labeled data is essential for training high-performance machine learning models. Crowdsourcing has been used successfully to obtain data annotations, yet it's worth noting that it's possible to leverage unlabeled data to improve efficiency. This strategy involves identifying and labeling only the most informative samples from the available data. This paper proposes a novel task combining machine learning and psychology, where volunteers are asked to watch a sequence of images and answer questions about specific pairs of images that are most likely to go together. To execute this task effectively, participants must learn meaningful relationships between samples, resulting in high-quality, targeted labels. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by showing that it results in labeling pairs of images most likely to be related, that volunteers are capable of answering our questions accurately, and that the proposed method results in labels that are highly correlated with random sampling but produce models that are significantly more efficient.

For the first time, neutron stars coming together while emitting both gravitational and electromagnetic radiation can be seen simultaneously, providing complete information about these events and greatly improving our understanding of neutron star mergers.

The pandemic's influence on urban diversity will vary greatly among different cities and communities in the future.  Initial observations suggest that avoidance of urban centers and reduced face-to-face interactions could harm our social resilience and diminish the richness of our lives.  However, obtaining quantitative data on these experiences and their impacts will be challenging in coming years.  Despite this, understanding how cities can foster resilience and promote diverse, low-carbon encounters is crucial for sustainable urban planning.  This presentation will explore the significance of urban diversity, the role of face-to-face encounters in our lives, and the potential for cities to foster sustainability.  It will also examine how to gather robust data to better inform policy decisions in the post-pandemic era.

A recent observation of the solar neighborhood object SS433 shows that the inner region of its surrounding system could be warmer, larger, and hotter than previously estimated. To verify this hypothesis, a computational model was created to account for the interaction between the inner system and any moving bodies within the outer system of this high mass young star. An initial least squares method was used to determine the outer system's distance, which was then used to find the temperature distribution of the warm region. The results show that the model accurately represents the movement of the system and the distribution of temperatures in the warm region. Additionally, the model indicates that the inner system's temperature range falls between previous estimates. The findings also suggest that similar interactions between young stars and migrating objects could help determine the stability of the systems around high mass young stars.

A numerical method based on a Green's function approach is developed to calculate
free surface elevation from the wave envelope in an inviscid water wave problem within
a channel. The proposed method is valid for amplitude obligations and involves
determining surface elevation as multiple times the depth of the water at multiple
positions. To handle nonlinear components, a second-order perturbation technique is
applied. With an example problem featuring partial water filling in a V-shaped
channel, approximate analytical solutions can be obtained and results from the
Green's function method match those from numerical integration.

A new theorem in differential geometry, termed the surface layer theorem, is demonstrated with a proof based on the retraction theorem, which relies on the concept of the barycentric map from a convex theorem, ultimately proving the equivalence of two definitions of closed differential forms in infinite-dimensional spacetime.

A novel sonar-based navigation system for mobile platforms is presented, featuring a sophisticated layered control design. The system consists of an outer layer utilizing raw sonar data for navigation decisions, a middle layer managing sonar placement through inverse kinematics, and an inner layer handling precise end-effector positioning with PID control. The proposed system was tested on a robotic vehicle equipped with a rotating sonar device, demonstrating its capability to navigate in unstructured environments and recover from failed maneuvers by dynamically reconfiguring the sensing pattern. Performance assessments highlight the system's capacity to efficiently utilize sonar data, minimize navigation failures, and enable adaptive behavior in response to sonar feedback.

This study presents a novel task called Multi-source Fake News Detection, which enhances existing single-source detection by incorporating context from various sources, such as other articles and social media posts, to improve the identification of counterfeit information. The challenge lies in dealing with inconsistent content across different sources, which can pose difficulties for current detection models. To address this issue, we developed three attention-based models that prioritize building contextual representations and facilitating effective interactions, allowing for more effective detection of counterfeit news. Our experimental results demonstrate that our approach, along with incorporating context, significantly surpasses traditional single-source detection baselines, showing a performance boost of 10 points on average. Additionally, we conducted a visual analysis that reveals our models' effectiveness in managing content discrepancies and reveals the limitations imposed by misleading information.

This research proposes a two-block $1$-norm optimization problem from the evaluation of rotationally invariant $L$-PCA in its subsequent formulation. Our approach, which can be categorized as an alternating minimization method, formulates two steps of iteration that respectively resolve tightly coupled sub-block variables independently from decoupled transformation matrices. Our solution leverages simple coordinate descent as the solving method for sub-block optimization problems and converges rapidly to an accurate approximation of the true PCA solution. Our convergent property has been theoretically confirmed, confirmed by numerical experiments comparing our method with existing alternative approaches, demonstrating significant convergence speed benefits, as well as significant performance gains in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy.

Semantics labeling consistency is a process where we check if the notes accompanying an edge in a knowledge graph can be described using the same term as the edges that connect the related entities.  The related edges form a triplet of entities and their accompanying notes.  We propose paraphrasing tasks to validate that our labels accurately capture the correct meaning and are useful for training AI models that can reason about graphs.  We develop a tool to create data for these tasks by generating potential paraphrases for each edge note, then filter out incorrect options.  We refine our results by having human annotators select the most appropriate label from the remaining options.  To show that our solution works, we incorporated the task into a loss function and a contrastive learning objective, which we did for the DoG graph embedding model.  Our approach yields an improvement in performance by nearly a factor of five compared to the baseline model.

Our new technique called HiTMap represents vehicles in a coordinate system that shifts with each other, similar to how we navigate in real life, to help self-driving cars move more efficiently. Unlike previous methodsHiTMap, the vehicle representation includes features to continuously track changes in the environment, allowing for precise estimates of speed and location in various scenarios, including temporary situations like parked cars. Our experiments show that HiTMap offers significant advantages over other approaches, such as a 40% improvement in navigation efficiency and better accuracy in locating vehicles, along with our findings showing HiTMap's effectiveness across different environments.

Using a two-pulse lattice structure with ultracold lithium atoms, the spectral range of magnetic field oscillations can be measured to very high precision through atomic interferometry. The proposed design allows the detection of minute local magnetic fields, as sensitive as $10^{-14}$ Tesla per root Hertz, while maintaining robustness against various sources of noise due to the width of the detected spectrum being thousands of times larger than the planetary Mollenauer-Bredt effect. Our calculations demonstrate that integrating measurements over a specific range of wavelengths could result in the possibility of detecting magnetic moments as small as $\sim0.3\hbarbar$ in a one-year observation.

We examine whether mixing proportions in finite mixture models are recoverable when using non-parametric methods, such as Dirichlet processes, and place non-parametric priors directly on probability density functions. Our findings reveal that methods disregarding the identification of group membership, like Dirichlet process mixtures, may fail to retrieve usable info from data, where even slight modifications can significantly alter the admissible admixture proportions. Notably, when employing Dirichlet process prior without ensuring the recoverability of admixture proportions in finite mixture models, we observed a substantial increase in the number of components needed to approximate the underlying distribution compared to using parametric methods, with little gain in model fit. Furthermore, when utilizing non-parametric methods based on resolving group membership, we found that the estimated number of components tended to be excessively numerous.

GPU programming relies heavily on effective memory allocation, with the choice of allocation method significantly impacting kernel launch overhead. Despite numerous available GPU memory allocators, each comes with its own performance and functionality trade-offs, making it challenging to allocate memory efficiently in complex applications. We developed DynaSOAr, an allocator that dynamically switches between different allocation strategies, tailored to the specific scenario at hand. Initially, we identified key parameters affecting kernel launch overhead, then tested multiple instances of allocation methods to identify the optimal configuration. We evaluated DynaSOAr against leading GPU memory allocators, and the results showed substantial improvements, including better overall runtime in a real application. Additionally, DynaSOAr demonstrates its utility in seamlessly meeting varied memory allocation requirements, potentially simplifying the complexity of GPU memory management.

We analyzed the interaction between a d-wave superconductor and in-plane magnetic adatoms or dimers on the surface of a material, focusing on the far from equilibrium state. The study found that the spin-orbit interaction allows for the tunneling of magnetic particles into quantum bound states, even within the superconducting region. Notably, in contrast to other scenarios, the peak positions of this phenomenon are insensitive to the strength of the spin-orbit coupling. Instead, it is the tunneling width that is affected by the spin-orbit coupling and local electron filling. When two atoms form a dimer in the atomic collapse state, they can exhibit both bonding and anti-bonding behavior. Furthermore, by manipulating the electron filling, researchers can induce a transition between these two states and thereby control the properties of the system.

A comprehensive study of the HATNet-POJ planet list, comprising 34 exoplanets found in eight distinct systems, reveals insights into the characteristics of transiting mini-Neptunes. These planets were primarily detected through the analysis of high-quality light curves obtained from automatic camera systems, with supplementary data from other observatories enabling precise atmospheric research. Notably, a unique discovery of four habitable zone planets exists within the list; these are classified as transiting mini-Neptunes and reside around low-mass M-dwarf stars. With further exploration using next-generation space telescopes, this discovery could provide an opportunity to understand potential sources of life.

The electronic structure of carbon and nitrogen within titanium dioxide (TiO2) was investigated through self-consistent first-principles calculations. Nitrogen and carbon exhibit distinct properties depending on their location in the crystal lattice. Substitutional nitrogen and carbon in the titanium site create localized states above the valence band maximum, with energies varying for N and C. Notably, nitrogen and carbon do not replace oxygen in the TiO2 lattice easily, as their localized states reside within the valence band, reducing their visibility. In contrast, interstitial nitrogen and carbon exhibit similar behavior with higher placement of their isolated states, placing them above the valence band maximum. The study also found that nitrogen and interstitial carbon in the titanium site possess a dipole moment along a specific crystallographic axis, whereas their other forms do not display this characteristic.

Top quark decays into other flavors are extremely uncommon and any observed instances would strongly suggest the top quark has some kind of intrinsic charm or charge-switching property. Using top quark pair productions along with $t\bar{t}$ resonance, our study explores flavor-changing neutral currents within the decay of top quarks into down-type quarks. By applying matrix element methods, we derived constraints on the branching fractions for $t\to dQ$ and $t\to sQ$ decays, which are found to be less than 0.44\times10^{-2} and 0.37\times10^{-2} at 95% confidence level, respectively, without considering detector effects. Additionally, more stringent limits were obtained for charged-current decays into down-type quarks, which are found to be less than 0.08 for both $t\to dW$ and $t\to sW$ branches, respectively.

We investigate mass determination in a periodic lattice with random site potentials, specifically a tight-binding lattice in $d$ dimensions with a three-level site, exhibiting a qubit or qutrit at each site. Each site can interact with the lattice and the site variables form a periodic pattern with period $L^d$. We examine local dephasing noise models for various site noises that don't scale with the lattice size. We establish error channels leading to quenching of coherence and determining mass tolerance thresholds for each channel, beyond which mass estimates diverge. Our analysis for both qubit and qutrit cases shows that noise tolerance is highest in the threshold dimension, exhibiting distinct dimensions for each channel and varying with the site noise model, but not the lattice dimension. Our findings for both qubit and qutrit cases are comparable, but generally noise tolerance in the mass estimate is higher in the qutrit model. Our results are presented for all dimensions $\ge 2$.

Recent measurements indicate that the polarization of a positron beam is approximately 10%, a limitation primarily imposed by the characteristics of the target used in the experimental setup. Overcoming this constraint is vital for developing potential applications requiring a higher positron polarization degree. Our research demonstrates achieving greater than 30% polarization in emitted positrons using a nanomesh target with an estimated areal density of 10^12 atoms per square厘米, which is substantially lower than traditional targets. Furthermore our findings suggest that such a low target density could result in an extremely useful beam with a notably higher flux of high-energy positrons.

We provide a comprehensive characterization of groups with polynomial diameter, especially concerning their conjugacy classes and nilpotent subgroups in their composition factors, effectively extending the findings of Guet and Wise.

This paper describes a new temperature sensor proposal with improved features, targeting better performance at a 12nm process node. The design achieves outstanding metrics with a resolution of down to 0.0154625 degrees Celsius and minimal inaccuracy of 0.298555555555556 degrees Celsius, at a low supply voltage of 1.1V. The proposed sensor outperforms usual specs in both resolution and inaccuracy, demonstrates reduced temperature range influence, and consumes less power than comparable designs, all while maintaining a simple circuitry and feedback mechanism.

Topological groupoid extensions form a structure that can be analyzed using the framework of topological stack cohomology, similarly to topological groupoid homology. Specifically, the "size" or dimension of a topological stack's gerbe-like entities of a certain complexity corresponds to the presence of non-zero values in that stack's associated cohomology. We establish this relationship by demonstrating the equivalence between the homology of an extension of a topological groupoid and its original groupoid, as well as the corresponding connection in the realm of cohomology, thereby solidifying the validity of computing the homology of abstract topological stacks through simplification complexes.

We investigated the mass development of molecular cores using the ALMA observatory, in an effort to clarify the formation process of massive stars. A sample of 524 molecular cores in 29 star-forming regions, tightly linked to massive star clusters, was examined. Linear regression analysis revealed that the mass growth rate of these cores varies significantly, from less than 0.01 Msun/year to over 10 Msun/year. The results show that in more than half of the observed cores, the mass growth pattern matches that of low-mass stars, while the remaining cores experienced passive gravitational collapse or mass loss. The research indicates that the majority of these cores will eventually give rise to massive stars or dense cores without disrupting a significant portion of their parent molecular clouds. Furthermore, we found that the molecular cores growth rate is directly correlated with their final mass and the mass growth rate of the surrounding molecular cloud. The ALMA observations provide a rare and comprehensive set of data on the mass growth characteristics of molecular cores in various stages of star formation, relevant to understanding the formation of massive stars.

We examine whether the process of differentiation or integration with respect to the angle between two vectors preserves the positive definiteness in a given zonal space. It has been proven by Schoenberg that both operations result in functions that are positively definite. However, the situation becomes more complex when considering partial integrations. Zonal spaces are defined based on the angle between two vectors in a given dimension, and they contain functions that exhibit positive definiteness and can be used to model similarity between pairs of vectors. The task at hand involves exploring the impact of integrating with respect to one of the angles on the preservation of positive definiteness. Initially, partial integrations are analyzed in straightforward coordinate systems in a given dimension, but a change of variable reveals their relevance to the angle between the two vectors. Ultimately, it is demonstrated that partial integrations also preserve positive definiteness in the angle between the two vectors. Furthermore, we provide a proof that classical differentiation and integration operations maintain the preservation of positive definiteness in the m-dimensional space. Additionally, we explore the connection between partial integrations and the preservation of positive definiteness in the angle between the two vectors.

A key parameter that is used to characterize the complexity of liquid foams is the roughness factor, which is defined as the ratio of the surface tension to the buoyancy force. In this study, we investigate how the presence of a boundary affects the ways in which foams flow by conducting numerical simulations in various geometric configurations including the Hele-Shaw cell, channel, and between parallel plates. To achieve this goal, level-set methods are used to perform detailed simulations of foams that allow us to compute the surface of the foam and its interaction with the surrounding geometry. By calculating the distribution functions of curvature and curvature intervals, we find curvature distributions that can help us to identify characteristic features of foam flow. Additionally, we discover a scaling law in the distribution of curvature intervals in the absence of geometric effects. Another finding is the relation of the roughness factor to the distribution of curvature intervals in the form of the relation of two power laws. In summary, our results provide new insights into the way in which liquid foams flow and the role that curvature plays in this process.

Recently, convolutional neural network ensemble methods have achieved record low errors in sensitive image classification benchmarks, yet the beneficial effects of ensembles are difficult to explain due to the intricate nature of individual neural networks. Our research proposes a simplified convolutional neural network ensemble that makes it possible to accurately describe the ensemble's performance, leveraging the accuracy of individual networks as a measure of difficulty. This approach allows us to track and anticipate the growing difficulty of real-world images despite the individual networks' limited capacity. Moreover, our network ensemble achieves results rivaling more complex and computationally expensive network ensembles.
